concept.name: Sortino ratio
concept.definition: A risk-adjusted performance measure that modifies the Sharpe ratio by penalizing only returns below a user-specified target (the minimum acceptable return): the excess of realized return over the target divided by the downside deviation (target semi-deviation).
concept.intuition: Upside volatility is profit, not danger; the Sortino ratio only charges the strategy for the harmful, below-target fluctuations.
concept.mechanics: Choose the target return T (e.g. 0% or the risk-free rate), compute the average realized excess over T and the downside deviation DR — the root of the probability-weighted squared below-target shortfalls — then divide. Developed by Frank Sortino and Brian Rom within post-modern portfolio theory.
concept.formula: S = (R - T) / DR, with DR = sqrt( integral_{-inf}^{T} (T - r)^2 f(r) dr ), where R is the average realized return, T the target (MAR), and f(r) the return distribution.
concept.failure_modes: Results hinge on the chosen target and on having enough below-target observations; short samples make DR statistically fragile. For near-symmetric distributions with T near the median it adds little over Sharpe, and discrete versus continuous conventions distort comparability.
concept.misconceptions: It is not Sharpe with a naive 'standard deviation of negative returns': the deviation is computed against a target across the whole distribution, and a higher Sortino than Sharpe does not mean the strategy is safer — only that its volatility skews to the upside.
concept.example: A strategy returning 28% annualized with a 7% downside deviation against a 5.25% target has a Sortino near 3.25 even though its total-volatility Sharpe is unimpressive — the classic asymmetric-payoff case.
